title: Permission Basics
lead: Read `ls -l` output and manage file and directory permissions correctly with `chmod`, `chown` and `umask`.
objectives: You read the type character, the three permission triplets, owner and group in `ls -l`.
You explain that r, w, x mean different things for files and for directories.
You know that deleting a file depends on the w+x permission of the **parent directory**, not of the file.
You set permissions with `chmod` (octal and symbolic) and change ownership with `chown`/`chgrp`.
You show by calculation that `umask` is a bit mask, not a subtraction.

sections.title: Reading ls -l output
body: `ls -l` prints one line per file: `-rw-r----- 1 student devs 120 Nov 12 10:00 report.txt`. The first character is the **type**: `-` file, `d` directory, `l` symbolic link. The next nine characters are three triplets: **owner (u)**, **group (g)**, **others (o)**. Each triplet is `rwx` for read, write, execute; a missing permission shows as `-`.

The two names after the number are owner and group (`student devs`); the `1` before them is the hard link count. The system checks in order: if you are the owner, only the owner triplet applies; otherwise, if you are in the group, the group triplet applies; otherwise the others triplet. **root** and processes with relevant capabilities can bypass many discretionary access-control (DAC) checks; other controls such as SELinux or a read-only mount may still deny access.
`id` shows your groups. A new group membership only reaches your process after a fresh login (or with `newgrp`).

commands.what: Lists files with type, permissions, owner, group, size and date.
commands.where: First stop for any permission problem.
commands.why: Shows at a glance who may do what.

commands.what: Shows the permissions of the directory itself (not its contents).
commands.why: `ls -l shared` lists the contents; for the directory itself you need `-d`.

commands.what: Shows file details; permissions in octal and symbolic form.
commands.where: When you want to verify the octal value.
commands.why: No need to convert between `ls -l` and octal in your head.

commands.where: For the question 'why can't I access this?'.
commands.why: Determines which triplet applies to you.

sections.tip: Split the permission string into groups of three: `rw- r-- ---` means owner reads and writes, group reads, others nothing.

sections.title: r, w, x: on files and on directories
body: **On files:** `r` reads the content, `w` changes the content, `x` runs the file as a program. New files are **never created executable**; for `./script.sh` you first need `chmod +x`.

**On directories:** `r` lists the names, `x` allows entering and reaching entries by name (`cd`, `cat vault/data.txt`), `w` allows creating, deleting and renaming entries. `w` alone is useless; **w needs x too**. To reach a path you need **x on every directory** along it.

**Key rule:** to delete or move a file, the file's own permissions do not matter; you need **w+x on the parent directory**. File permissions only control reading and writing the content. So a `644` file inside a `555` directory cannot be deleted, and neither can a `777` file there.

commands.what: Reads file content; needs r on the file and x on the directories in the path.
Deletes a file; success depends on w+x of the parent directory.
commands.why: The directory permission decides, not the file permission.

commands.what: Enters a directory; needs x on the directory.
commands.why: Without x you cannot get in.

sections.tip: When you say 'I can't delete it', don't look at the file; look at the **directory** with `ls -ld .`.
sections.warn: `chmod -R 777` is not a fix. It gives everyone write and execute rights, hides the real cause and opens a security hole. First find the real reason with `ls -l` and `id`.

sections.title: chmod: changing permissions
body: In octal notation you add **r=4, w=2, x=1**: `7`=rwx, `6`=rw-, `5`=r-x, `4`=r--, `0`=---. The three digits are for owner, group, others. Common values: `644` (regular file), `755` (program and directory), `600` (private file), `700` (private directory), `664` and `775` (group work).

In symbolic notation you write who (`u`, `g`, `o`, `a`), operation (`+`, `-`, `=`) and permission (`r`, `w`, `x`): `chmod g+w,o-rx shared`. **Capital `X`** sets x only on directories and on files that are already executable; `chmod -R u=rwX,go=rX data` makes directories 755 and previously non-executable files 644, while preserving x on files that were already executable.
Only the **owner** (or root) may change permissions; on someone else's file you get `Operation not permitted`.

commands.what: Sets octal permissions: owner rw-, group r--, others ---.
commands.where: When you define permissions in one step.
commands.why: The result is explicit and repeatable.
Changes only x, leaves other bits (subject to umask).

commands.what: Symbolic: group gains write, others lose read and execute.
commands.why: Changes only the bits you name.

commands.what: Fixes a tree recursively: files 644, directories 755.
commands.why: Thanks to `X`, files don't get needless x.

sections.tip: Look at the target with `ls -l` first; with `-R`, double-check the end of the path.
sections.danger: Running `chmod -R` with a wrong value on `/` or `~` breaks the system or your home (e.g. SSH key permissions, sudo). In the VM take a **snapshot** first and work only inside the practice folder.

sections.title: chown and chgrp: owner and group
body: Every file has an owner and a group. **Only root may change the owner** (`sudo chown`). A regular user may only set a file's group to a group they belong to; in the simulator we use `sudo chgrp` for that.

`chown alice:devs report.txt` sets owner and group together. A typical team setup: group `devs`, mode `660` on files or `770` on directories; only `devs` members get access. Finer rules (per-user permissions) use ACLs (`getfacl`/`setfacl`); those come in later modules.

commands.what: Changes the owner (and optionally the group).
commands.where: When handing a file over to another user.
When assigning a group to a shared directory.
commands.why: Keeps the owner and controls group access.

sections.tip: Be careful with `chown -R` on real systems too; verify the path with `ls -ld` first.

sections.title: umask: default permissions
body: New files **start** from `666`, new directories from `777`; `umask` removes bits using a **mask**: **new mode = base & ~umask**. This is not subtraction. Examples (file, base 666): umask `022` → `644`; `027` → `640`; `077` → `600`; `002` → `664`.

The difference shows when the umask has bits the base lacks: for `025`, `666 & ~025 = 642`, while subtraction would give `641` (wrong). For `001` the result is `666`, subtraction would give `665`. Because x is not in the base, files are never created executable.
`umask` is **per process**: it applies only in that shell and the programs started from it. To make it permanent, put it in `~/.bashrc` (user) or `/etc/profile` (system).

commands.what: Shows the current mask in octal (e.g. `0022`).
commands.where: To understand permissions of new files.
commands.why: Explains why files are created as 644.

commands.where: When you want to see the allowed bits directly.
commands.why: Shows what is granted instead of what is removed.

commands.what: Sets the mask for this shell: new files 640, directories 750.
commands.why: Affects every new file that follows.

sections.tip: In shared project folders use `umask 002`: new files `664`, directories `775`.

t01.text: List the permissions of the files in the `lab` folder with `ls -l`.
t01.hint: Read the first 10 characters of each line: type + three triplets.

t02.hint: Then check the x bits with `ls -l script.sh`.

t04.text: Run `chmod 640 notes.txt` so the owner has rw-, group r--, others ---.

t05.text: Set the `shared` directory to `770` symbolically: add write for the group, remove read and execute from others (`chmod g+w,o-rx shared`).
t05.hint: Separate the two operations with a comma, no space.

t06.text: Make `alice` the owner of `team.txt` with `sudo chown alice team.txt`.
t06.hint: Only root can change the owner, so `sudo` is needed.

t07.text: Set the group of `team.txt` to `devs` with `sudo chgrp devs team.txt`.

t08.text: Set `umask 027`, then create a file with `touch new.txt`. What permissions does it get?

t09.text: Predict: `locked` is `555`, and `old.txt` inside is `644`. Does `rm locked/old.txt` work? Run it to check.
t09.hint: Deleting needs w on the directory; look with `ls -ld locked`.

t10.text: Predict: what mode does `predict.txt` get after `umask 025` and `touch predict.txt`? Calculate first (666 & ~025), then run it and verify with `ls -l predict.txt`.
t10.hint: Subtraction gives 641; the correct mask calculation gives 642.

t11.text: Predict: does `./deploy.sh` run? Run it to check.
t11.hint: The file is 644 with no x bit: expect `Permission denied`.

t12.text: Debug: `locked/old.txt` cannot be deleted. Fix the problem and delete the file.
t12.hint: Look at the directory, not the file: `chmod u+w locked`, then `rm`.

t13.text: Debug: `cat vault/data.txt` fails. Fix it and read the file.
t13.hint: `vault` is `600`: no x, you cannot get in. `chmod u+x vault`.

t14.text: Mini project: create a `team` directory with `plan.txt` inside; directory `770`, file `660`; set the directory's group to `devs` with `sudo chgrp devs team`.

t15.text: Challenge: everything in the `data` tree is `777`. Make directories `755` and files `644` (`data/a.txt`, `data/sub/b.txt`).

t16.text: TICKET #4401 — Alice will edit `report.txt`, group `devs` may write too, nobody else gets access. Set owner `alice`, group `devs`, mode `660`.
t16.hint: First `chmod 660`, then `sudo chown alice:devs`; after the owner changes you can no longer run chmod.

t17.text: TICKET #4402 — The team creates new files in `shared` and the group cannot write them. Set `umask 002` and create a `664` file with `touch shared/log.txt`.

vm.intro: Work in your own VM inside the `~/permlab` practice folder. Paste the commands in order and paste the output on this page. Take a snapshot before destructive steps.

v01.title: Read permissions
v01.text: Read the permission strings of system files and check your identity.

blocks.expected:
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  2345 Nov 12 10:00 /etc/passwd
-rw-r----- 1 root shadow 1234 Nov 12 10:00 /etc/shadow
-rwsr-xr-x 1 root root 59976 Nov 12 10:00 /usr/bin/passwd
drwxrwxrwt 15 root root 4096 Nov 12 10:00 /tmp

differs: On Rocky/Alma `/etc/shadow` may show `----------`; that is normal (root bypasses the check).
`s` (setuid) and `t` (sticky) are special bits; for now just treat them as 'x-like'.

v02.title: Practice with chmod
v02.text: Create the practice folder and a file, set the mode to `640` and show the result.

blocks.cmd:
mkdir -p ~/permlab
cd ~/permlab
touch notes.txt
chmod 640 notes.txt
ls -l notes.txt
stat -c '%a %A %U:%G' notes.txt

differs: `stat -c` exists only in GNU stat; it does not work on macOS/BSD, you can ignore it.
If your user is not `student`, you will see your own name; that is fine.

v03.title: Deleting depends on directory permission
v03.text: Set the directory to `555`, try to delete the file inside, then restore the directory permission.

blocks.cmd:
cd ~/permlab
mkdir locked
touch locked/old.txt
chmod 555 locked
rm locked/old.txt
ls -ld locked
chmod 755 locked
rm locked/old.txt
ls locked
blocks.expected:
rm: cannot remove 'locked/old.txt': Permission denied
dr-xr-xr-x 2 student student 4096 Nov 12 10:00 locked

differs: As root the delete succeeds because root bypasses permissions; test as a normal user.
The message may be translated (`Zugriff verweigert`, `Erişim engellendi`).

v04.title: Effect of umask
v04.text: Set the mask to `027` and look at the permissions of a new file and a new directory. Note: this change affects only this terminal session.

blocks.cmd:
cd ~/permlab
umask
umask 027
touch f027.txt
mkdir d027
ls -ld f027.txt d027
umask 022
blocks.expected:
0022
-rw-r----- 1 student student 0 Nov 12 10:00 f027.txt
drwxr-x--- 2 student student 4096 Nov 12 10:00 d027

differs: Your starting umask may be `0002` (Ubuntu with a per-user group); that is normal.
In a new terminal the old value returns: umask is per process.

v05.title: chown and cleanup
v05.text: Make root the owner of the file, then delete the directory: since you may write to the parent directory, the root-owned file is deleted too.

blocks.cmd:
cd ~/permlab
touch owned.txt
sudo chown root:root owned.txt
ls -l owned.txt
cd ~
rm -r ~/permlab
ls ~/permlab
blocks.expected:
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 0 Nov 12 10:00 owned.txt
ls: cannot access '/home/student/permlab': No such file or directory

differs: If `sudo` asks for a password, enter your own.
If `rm: remove write-protected regular file?` appears, type `y`: deleting the root-owned file depends on the directory permission, not the file permission.
Type the `rm -r` path carefully; never try it on `/` or `~`.

q1.q: Which permission is needed to delete `notes.txt`?
options: w and x on the parent directory
q1.explain: Deleting removes the directory entry, so you need w+x on the parent directory. The file's own permission does not decide.

q2.q: With `umask 027`, what mode does a new file get?

q3.q: What does `x` on a directory allow?
options: Entering it and reaching entries by name
q3.explain: x on a directory is the traverse permission (`cd`, passing through a path). Listing needs r.

q4.q: Why is `chmod -R 777` the wrong fix for 'Permission denied'?
options: It gives everyone full access and hides the real cause
q4.explain: 777 grants everyone read, write and execute and weakens security. First find the cause with `ls -l` and `id`, then grant only the minimum needed.

summary: `ls -l`: type character + owner/group/others triplets; r=4, w=2, x=1.
On directories: r=list, w=create/delete/rename (with x), x=enter/access; deleting a file depends on w+x of its parent directory.
`chmod` works in octal (`640`) or symbolic (`g+w`, `u=rwX`); only root can `chown`.
umask is a mask, not a subtraction: new mode = base & ~umask (file 666, directory 777).
`chmod -R 777` is not a fix; apply the principle of least privilege.

glossary.meaning: A separate rwx set for owner, group and others.
Permissions written as the sum r=4, w=2, x=1, e.g. 644.
Bit mask that defines which permission bits are removed from new files and directories.
The user the file belongs to; may change permissions.
A set of users sharing permissions, e.g. devs.
The x bit on a directory; allows passing through the path and access by name.
